# High Desert Development

General contractor. Antelope Valley and High Desert, California.
California Contractors State License Board license 771814. Licensed, bonded and insured.
In business since 1999. Owner: Jerry Heller.
Phone: 760-382-2658
Website: https://highdesertdevelopment.com/

## What is distinctive

The owner is on every job. He runs the work on site rather than handing it to a
project manager, and the trades are kept in house rather than bid out job to
job. The same crew that digs the utilities pours the foundation and frames the
walls, so there is one company and one person answerable for the whole build.
He is also a certified home inspector, and he checks his own crews' work the
way an inspector checks a finished house.

## Service area

The Antelope Valley, the Victor Valley and the Kern River Valley, roughly a
hundred miles in every direction from California City, across Kern,
Los Angeles and San Bernardino counties. This includes Lancaster, Palmdale,
Rosamond, Mojave, Tehachapi, California City, Boron, Edwards AFB, Ridgecrest,
Inyokern, Bakersfield, Lake Isabella, Acton, Littlerock, Pearblossom, Quartz
Hill, Lake Los Angeles, Sun Village, Agua Dulce, Leona Valley, Santa Clarita,
Altadena, Adelanto, Victorville, Apple Valley, Hesperia, Barstow and
Wrightwood.

## Services

- Underground utilities: wet and dry utilities, deep wells, sewer and septic
  systems, trenching, land clearing and site preparation
- New residential construction: custom homes built from bare ground up
- Custom ADUs and pool houses
- Commercial construction: build-outs, wood framing, ground-up commercial
- Concrete and masonry: foundations, slabs, driveways, patios, walkways, block
  walls, stamped and colored decorative concrete
- Remodeling: kitchens, bathrooms and custom showers, fireplaces, room
  additions, home extensions, roofing in tile and composition shingle
- Sports courts: pickleball, tennis and basketball, indoor or outdoor. Very few
  contractors in this area take this work on.

## Financing

Construction financing is available on custom homes, ADUs and larger projects.
Construction loans are paid out in stages as work is completed rather than in
one lump, and during the build most borrowers pay interest only on the amount
drawn so far. Most construction loans written for an owner-occupied home are
construction-to-permanent loans, which convert into an ordinary long-term
mortgage when the house is finished, with one application and one closing. The
specifics depend on the lender, so ask before signing.

## Building on vacant land

A large amount of High Desert land was sold decades ago and never built on.
Whether a parcel can be built on comes down to four questions: is it a legal lot
zoned for a dwelling with recorded access, can water reach it or does it need a
well, can power reach it or is solar the better option, and will the soil take a
septic system. Those answers move the cost of a build more than the house design
does, and they can be established from a parcel number before any money is spent
on plans. See https://highdesertdevelopment.com/cost-to-build-on-a-lot

## Rebuilding after a fire

Rebuild work is taken on, including Altadena and the foothill communities. A lot
that had a house on it is already an established building site, so the open
questions are different from raw land: whether the foundation survived the heat,
which an engineer establishes rather than a site walk, and what condition the
sewer or septic connection, water service and conduit runs are in. Site
clearance has to be completed and documented before anything is permitted, and
Los Angeles County publishes the current requirements at
https://recovery.lacounty.gov/rebuilding/. Rebuilding close to the footprint,
size and design of the house that was lost goes through a faster permit route
than a redesign. A house rebuilt in a high fire hazard zone has to meet
California's wildfire construction standards on ignition-resistant or
noncombustible exterior materials and ember-resistant vents; guides written
before 2026 call this Chapter 7A of the building code, and those provisions now
sit in the California Wildland-Urban Interface Code.

California treats rebuilding a home as home improvement work, so four contract
rules apply: the deposit cannot exceed $1,000 or 10 percent of the contract
price, whichever is less; the right to cancel is seven business days rather than
three where a state or local emergency was declared for the event that damaged
the property; the contract must state a fixed total price and a payment schedule
in dollars, which time and materials and cost plus do not; and change orders are
signed before the work. Any contractor's licence can be checked free at
https://www.cslb.ca.gov/OnlineServices/CheckLicenseII/CheckLicense.aspx
See https://highdesertdevelopment.com/rebuilding-after-a-fire
